'''''Kolkwitzia amabilis''''' {{IPAc-en|k|ɒ|l|ˈ|k|w|ɪ|t|s|i|ə|_|ə|ˈ|m|æ|b|ᵻ|l|ɪ|s}},<ref>''Sunset Western Garden Book,'' 1995:606–607</ref> commonly known as '''beauty bush''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Caprifoliaceae]]. It is the sole species in genus '''''Kolkwitzia'''''.<ref name = powo/> It is a [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] grown as an [[ornamental plant]]. In China, where it originated, the plant is called ''wèi shí shù<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.shutterstock.com/search/wei+shi+shu|title = Wei Shi Shu Images, Stock Photos & Vectors | Shutterstock}}</ref>'' (蝟实树).<ref>{{cite web |publisher=Harvard University Herbaria |url=http://flora.huh.harvard.edu/china/PDF/PDF19/Kolkwitzia.pdf |title=4. KOLKWITZIA Graebner, Bot. Jahrb. Syst. 29: 593. 1901.}}</ref>

==Description==
[[Image:Kolkwitzia amabilis5.jpg|thumb|Flower]]
The plant is an arching, spreading shrub, with light brown flaky bark and graceful arching branches, which can grow higher than {{cvt|8|ft|m|1}} tall. It is usually as wide as it is tall.  The plant blooms in late spring.  Its light pink flowers, dark pink in the bud, are about one-inch long and bell-shaped ("tubular campanulate"); they grow in pairs, as with all Caprifoliaceae, and form showy, numerous sprays along ripened wood. Its leaves are opposite, simple, and ovate, from {{cvt|0.5|to|3|in|cm}} long, entire or with a few sparse shallow teeth.  Its fruit is a hairy, ovoid capsule approximately {{cvt|0.25|in|cm|1}} inches long.{{citation needed|date=June 2017}}

==Taxonomy==
The species was first described by [[Paul Graebner]] and placed in the new genus ''Kolkwitzia'', whose name honours [[Richard Kolkwitz]], a professor of botany in Berlin.<ref>{{cite book | last = Albert | first = Render | editor=L.H. Bailey | title = The Standard Cyclopedia of Horticulture | publisher = MacMillan & Co., Ltd. | year = 1917 | location = London | pages = [https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_72EDAAAAMAAJ/page/n603 1757] | url = https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_72EDAAAAMAAJ | quote = Kolkwitzia amabilis. }}</ref> The [[Botanical name#Components of plant names|specific epithet]] ''amabilis'' means "lovely".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for gardeners |year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |location=United Kingdom |isbn=9781845337315 |pages=224}}</ref>

==History==
The beauty bush originates in Central China, where it has been discovered for western science twice; once by the Jesuit missionary Giuseppe Giraldi in [[Shaanxi]], and then in western [[Hubei|Hubei province]] by the British explorer and plant collector [[Ernest Henry Wilson|E.H. Wilson]].<ref>[http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/~gdk/stabotanic/jun05pom.htm St Andrews Botanical Garden: ''Kolkwitzia amabilis''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080626193306/http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/~gdk/stabotanic/jun05pom.htm |date=2008-06-26 }}</ref> Wilson sent plant material to his sponsors Veitch Nurseries in [[Exeter]] in 1901, where the shrub flowered for the first time in 1910.<ref>Alice M. Coats, ''Garden Shrubs and Their Histories'' (1964) 1992, ''s.v.'' "Kolkwitzia"</ref> The shrub became very popular in the eastern United States following World War I – almost a defining shrub in American gardens made between the World Wars. It is very rare and threatened in the wild.

==Cultivation==
Numerous cultivars have been developed for garden use. The cultivar 'Pink Cloud' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/67708/Kolkwitzia-amabilis-Pink-Cloud/Details | title = '''Kolkwitzia amabilis'' 'Pink Cloud' | publisher = RHS | website = www.rhs.org | access-date = 3 September 2019}}</ref> 
<ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 57 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | website = www.rhs.org | access-date = 17 March 2018}}</ref>

===Pruning===
Opinions differ concerning how much pruning the shrub needs. The University of Missouri Horticulture Department suggests minimal intervention, so long as the plant has enough room to develop, up to a maximum height of {{cvt|15|ft|m}} and a potential "spread" of {{cvt|8|ft|m}}.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Selecting Landscape Plants: Deciduous Shrubs|url=http://hdl.handle.net/10919/23460|journal=Department of Horticulture, University of Missouri|year=2000|hdl=10919/23460|last1=Relf|first1=Diane|last2=Appleton|first2=Bonnie Lee}}</ref> Others suggest more active intervention to encourage development of new flowering branches and buds, with decisive pruning immediately after flowering.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Pruning Kolkwitzia amabilis - How/when to prune Beauty Bush |date=23 June 2020 |url=https://www.gardenseeker.com/pruning/pruning_kolkwitzia.htm}}</ref>
